clues: I am an indentation in a coastline filled with sea or lake water.
Land curves around my water, leaving an opening to the larger waterbody.
San Francisco has a famous example of this coastal water feature.
quest.example: San Francisco Bay curves into the land.

clues: I am a strip of loose sand, pebbles, or shells beside water.
Waves and currents move the loose material along my edge.
Look for a gently sloping place where land meets a lake or sea, not a sheltered water basin.
quest.example: A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida.

clues: My everyday name often describes a small stream.
The word is common for a modest watercourse running between banks.
Creek and stream overlap with my meaning, so size alone cannot uniquely distinguish us.
quest.example: A little brook bubbles over pebbles.
quest.note: Creek and stream overlap with my meaning, so size alone cannot uniquely distinguish us.

clues: I am a projecting point of land at a coast.
My point extends into a sea, ocean, or lake.
Headland overlaps with my meaning; there is no universal separation between the names.
quest.example: Cape Cod reaches out into the Atlantic Ocean.
quest.note: Headland overlaps with my meaning; there is no universal separation between the names.

clues: I am the zone where land borders an ocean or sea.
Beaches, cliffs, and estuaries can all occur along me.
Shore is a broader overlapping word; my name usually points specifically to the sea.
quest.example: Florida's Atlantic coast is next to the ocean.
quest.note: Shore is a broader overlapping word; my name usually points specifically to the sea.

clues: I am a relatively small, sheltered coastal indentation or bay.
Land or headlands can protect my water from some open-water waves.
My name is often used for a sheltered inlet, not an island.
quest.example: A small sheltered cove might hold tiny boats.

clues: My everyday name often describes a relatively small natural watercourse.
People in different regions use my name differently.
Stream and brook may be equally reasonable names for the same flowing water.
quest.example: A creek winds past trees and rocks.

clues: I am water moving in a particular direction.
I can transport floating objects through a river or ocean.
I describe water's directed flow, not a floating piece of ice or an apparent skyline.
quest.example: An ocean current carries water along the coast.

clues: I am a deposit of river-carried sediment near some river mouths.
Sediment builds up where flowing water slows enough to leave material behind.
Not every river mouth forms me, and I need not be a perfect triangle.
quest.example: The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf.

clues: I describe travel in the direction a watercourse flows.
I point toward its mouth rather than its headwaters.
I am a direction, not the place where the river begins.
quest.example: A floating leaf goes downstream with the current.

clues: The Gulf of Mexico bears my conventional waterbody name.
I am an arm of the sea partly enclosed by land.
Bay and gulf overlap; there is no universal size rule that distinguishes them.
quest.example: The Gulf of Mexico is partly surrounded by land.
quest.note: Bay and gulf overlap; there is no universal size rule that distinguishes them.

clues: I am a sheltered water area where vessels can anchor or find refuge.
I may be naturally sheltered or protected by built structures.
A pier or wharf can stand within me, but is not the water area itself.
quest.example: New York Harbor provides sheltered water for ships.

clues: Water surrounds this separate piece of land on every side.
Unlike a peninsula, I have no above-water connection to a larger landmass.
Madagascar is a large example.
quest.example: Hawaii has many islands surrounded by ocean.

clues: I am a narrow strip of land connecting two larger land areas.
Water lies on two sides of my land connection.
Panama is a famous example; I am land rather than a water passage.
quest.example: The Isthmus of Panama links two larger land areas.

clues: Lake Superior and Lake Victoria belong to my category of inland waterbodies.
Land encloses my water, apart from any inlets and outlets.
My name is commonly used for larger inland waterbodies; the boundary with ponds is not universal.
quest.example: Lake Michigan is a very large lake.
quest.note: My name is commonly used for larger inland waterbodies; the boundary with ponds is not universal.

clues: I am one of Earth's vast, connected bodies of salt water.
The Pacific is the largest named example of my category.
Together my connected waters cover most of Earth's surface.
quest.example: The Pacific Ocean covers a huge part of Earth.

clues: I am a projection of land with water on most sides and a land connection remaining.
Unlike an island, I am attached to a larger land area.
Florida is a familiar example of my shape.
quest.example: Florida sticks out into the Atlantic and Gulf waters.

clues: In everyday language, I am a relatively small, often shallow pool of still inland water.
A small garden waterbody with ducks or water lilies is often given my name.
My name overlaps with lake; there is no universal size rule separating us.
quest.example: A duck pond in a neighborhood park.
quest.note: My name overlaps with lake; there is no universal size rule separating us.

clues: I am a turbulent, fast-flowing stretch of a river or stream.
Rocks, channel shape, and a steep gradient can create my rough water.
I describe a rough reach of water, rather than one distinct waterfall drop.
quest.example: Whitewater rapids tumble over rocks in rivers.

clues: I am a ridge or raised feature of rock, coral, or other material in water.
My top lies at or near the surface in many examples.
Coral-built examples provide habitat, but not all reefs are coral reefs.
quest.example: Colorful coral reefs grow in warm tropical seas.

clues: I am a natural channel carrying flowing water across land.
The Amazon and Nile are named examples of my category.
I carry water toward another river, a lake, or the sea; I am not the direction of travel.
quest.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States.

clues: I name the place where a river enters another waterbody.
A river may enter a lake, another river, or the sea here.
A delta may form near me, but many river mouths have no delta.
quest.example: The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

clues: I name the beginning or headwaters of a river.
A spring, lake, glacier, or several small streams can supply me.
I am the starting location, not the direction upstream itself.
quest.example: A mountain spring may be a river's source.

clues: The Mediterranean is a named example of my category of salt water.
I am connected to the world ocean and may be partly enclosed by land.
My name is a conventional waterbody name, not a rule about one exact size.
quest.example: The Mediterranean Sea lies between Europe and Africa.

clues: I am land immediately beside a body of water.
You can find me beside an ocean, lake, or river.
A shoreline is the boundary line; I describe the adjoining strip or area of land.
quest.example: The shore of a lake is where its water meets land.

clues: I mark the boundary where water meets land.
My position can shift as water levels or tides change.
I describe an edge or line, rather than the whole neighboring shore area.
quest.example: A lake's shoreline curves around its edges.

clues: I am a general term for a natural flow of water in a channel.
Rivers, brooks, and creeks can all be described by my broad category.
Those flowing-water names overlap; my word does not require one fixed size.
quest.example: A small stream runs through a wooded park.
quest.note: Those flowing-water names overlap; my word does not require one fixed size.

clues: My defining relationship is that I flow into another stream or river.
I can myself be a stream or river; being small is not the defining rule.
My water joins the receiving watercourse rather than flowing out of it.
quest.example: The Missouri River joins the Mississippi River.

clues: I describe travel against a watercourse's flow.
I point toward its headwaters rather than its mouth.
I am a direction, not a sediment-built landform.
quest.example: A canoe going upstream travels toward a river's start.

clues: I occur where flowing water drops abruptly over an edge.
Water descends from an upper channel to a lower level.
Unlike a stretch of rapids, I include a distinct drop or series of drops.
quest.example: Niagara Falls pours over a steep drop.

clues: My water rotates around a center.
Meeting currents or obstructions can help produce my swirling movement.
I am a rotating flow pattern, rather than a chamber that raises boats.
quest.example: Water can spin in a whirlpool near rocks.

clues: I am a deep valley with steep sides, often cut by running water.
Arizona's Grand Canyon is a named example.
Gorge overlaps with my meaning; my name does not follow a universal width cutoff.
quest.example: The Grand Canyon has deep sides carved by a river.
quest.note: Gorge overlaps with my meaning; my name does not follow a universal width cutoff.

clues: I am a natural opening or cavity in rock large enough to enter.
Dissolving limestone can create one kind of me; lava can create another.
My interior may extend underground, but not every cave is below the surface.
quest.example: Mammoth Cave has underground passages.

clues: I am a very steep rock or earth face.
I may border a coast, valley, or plateau.
A bluff can be a kind of steep bank or cliff; that overlap is not a reason to mark bluff wrong.
quest.example: The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.
quest.note: A bluff can be a kind of steep bank or cliff; that overlap is not a reason to mark bluff wrong.

clues: I am a bowl-shaped depression associated with an impact or volcanic activity.
A meteorite impact can form me; a volcanic opening can also have my shape.
I am the hollow, not a hill of windblown sand.
quest.example: A volcano may have a bowl-shaped crater at its top.

clues: I am a mound or ridge of sand shaped chiefly by wind.
You can find me in deserts and beside some coasts.
Wind deposits and reshapes my sand.
quest.example: Sand dunes rise in Colorado's Great Sand Dunes.

clues: I am a persistent mass of land ice that moves under its own weight.
Snow accumulates and compresses into the ice that feeds me.
I flow over land; an iceberg is a detached floating piece of ice.
quest.example: A glacier slowly moves down an Alaskan valley.

clues: I am a raised landform often described as lower or less imposing than a mountain.
My shape may be rounded, but that is not a universal rule.
My name is conventional: there is no single worldwide height limit for hills.
quest.example: A rounded grassy hill in a park.

clues: I am a detached mass of freshwater ice floating in water.
I can break off from a glacier or an ice shelf.
Most of my volume usually lies below the water surface.
quest.example: Icebergs float in the cold North Atlantic Ocean.

clues: I am the solid terrestrial part of Earth's surface, contrasted with bodies of water.
I can include soil, rock, plains, and mountains.
My word is a broad category, not one particular field or wetland.
quest.example: A grassy farm is one part of Earth's land.

clues: The Himalayas contain many of my high, prominent landforms.
I rise strongly above the surrounding terrain and may have ridges and a summit.
The boundary between my name and hill varies; no single worldwide height rule applies.
quest.example: Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas.

clues: I am a group or chain of related mountains.
Several summits and valleys can occur within my larger highland system.
The Andes are a named example of my category.
quest.example: The Rocky Mountains are a mountain range.

clues: I am a place with a reliable water source within an otherwise dry region.
My water can support vegetation and human settlement.
I am not the whole desert; I am a watered location within it.
quest.example: An oasis may have palms and a pool in a desert.

clues: I am a high point, often a pointed top, on a mountain or ridge.
A mountain can have several of me, with one being its highest summit.
Peak and summit overlap; I am not defined by a different universal height.
quest.example: A pointed mountain peak sticks up into the clouds.
quest.note: Peak and summit overlap; I am not defined by a different universal height.

clues: I am a broad area with relatively low relief.
My surface is level or gently rolling compared with rugged mountain terrain.
I need not be at sea level; my broad, fairly even surface is the key clue.
quest.example: The Great Plains spread across central North America.

clues: I am a broad elevated area with a relatively level surface.
My surface stands above some neighboring terrain.
A mesa can resemble a smaller isolated example; size naming is not universal.
quest.example: The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.
quest.note: A mesa can resemble a smaller isolated example; size naming is not universal.

clues: I am an elongated crest of raised ground.
My narrow high line may connect several summits.
Lower land usually lies on either side of my crest.
quest.example: A ridge can run along the top of a mountain.

clues: I describe a surface's incline or gradient.
A hillside can have a gentle or steep version of me.
I describe how ground tilts, rather than a separate mountain group.
quest.example: Skiers travel downhill on a snowy slope.

clues: I am the highest point of a mountain or another elevated feature.
Climbers may aim to stand at me.
Peak sometimes overlaps with my meaning; a highest point can be rounded or pointed.
quest.example: A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit.
quest.note: Peak sometimes overlaps with my meaning; a highest point can be rounded or pointed.

clues: I am an elongated low area between higher hills or mountains.
A river may follow my floor, or a glacier may have widened me.
My defining feature is the low corridor between higher sides, not a summit.
quest.example: Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls.

clues: I am a vent, or a landform around a vent, through which magma may reach the surface.
Eruptions can release lava, gas, and ash.
I need not look like a tall cone, and not every mountain is one of me.
quest.example: Mount St. Helens in Washington is a volcano.

clues: My defining climate feature is very low precipitation.
I can be cold as well as hot; Antarctica contains an enormous example.
Sparse rainfall, not the presence of sand or cactus, defines my dry environment.
quest.example: The Sahara Desert receives very little rainfall.

clues: I am an open land area that may be managed for crops or another use.
A farmer might plant wheat in me, or people might use me for a sport.
My name describes an open area or its use, not a landform defined by height.
quest.example: A grassy field where children play soccer.

clues: I am a land area dominated by trees.
My trees form habitat for animals, fungi, and smaller plants.
Woodland and woods overlap with my meaning; they are not automatically wrong names.
quest.example: The Amazon Rainforest has millions of trees.
quest.note: Woodland and woods overlap with my meaning; they are not automatically wrong names.

clues: I am a wetland dominated mainly by grasses, reeds, sedges, or similar nonwoody plants.
My ground is saturated or periodically covered by shallow water.
Trees are not my dominant vegetation; that helps compare me with many swamps.
quest.example: Grassy marshes grow in the Florida Everglades.

clues: I am open land mainly covered by grasses and other soft-stemmed plants.
Wildflowers may grow among my grasses; grazing or mowing can help maintain me.
I can be a kind of field, so the words are not strict opposites.
quest.example: A meadow covered in grass and wildflowers.

clues: I am naturally occurring material or energy that people can use.
Fresh water, timber, minerals, and sunlight can be examples.
I am a use-related category; one example is not the whole category.
quest.example: Freshwater, trees, and stone can be useful resources.

clues: I am a natural mixture of minerals, organic material, air, and water near the land surface.
Roots often grow through me and organisms help form me.
I am more specific than land or earth in general.
quest.example: Roots grow down into dark, crumbly soil.

clues: I am a wetland in which trees or shrubs are prominent.
Standing or slow-moving water may surround my woody vegetation.
I differ from a typical marsh in the dominant vegetation, not merely in being wet.
quest.example: Cypress trees can grow in a flooded swamp.

clues: I am the collective plant cover in a place.
Grasses, shrubs, and trees are all parts of me.
I name the plants themselves, rather than the ground they grow in.
quest.example: Grass, bushes, and trees are all vegetation.

clues: My everyday name describes an area with many trees.
People may use my name for a smaller wooded area, but size is not a fixed rule.
My meaning overlaps with woodland and forest.
quest.example: A small patch of woods behind a house.
quest.note: My meaning overlaps with woodland and forest.

clues: I am a waterway built or substantially modified by people.
People may use me for transport, irrigation, or drainage.
The Panama waterway is a famous example of my category.
quest.example: Ships travel through the Panama Canal.

clues: Japan and Brazil are examples of my political category.
A government governs territory within my borders.
I am a political unit, rather than a natural landform.
quest.example: Brazil is a country in South America.

clues: I am a barrier built across a watercourse to hold back or control water.
Water stored behind me can form a reservoir.
I cross the flow; a flood levee usually runs alongside it.
quest.example: Hoover Dam holds back water in a river.

clues: I am a built platform commonly projecting from land out over water.
Piles or other supports hold my deck above the water.
Wharf can overlap with my meaning; these structures are named differently in different ports.
quest.example: A fishing pier reaches out over the ocean.
quest.note: Wharf can overlap with my meaning; these structures are named differently in different ports.

clues: I am a passage through or beneath an obstruction.
People build many of me for roads, trains, or water, although natural tunnels also exist.
I describe a through-passage rather than an elevated flat area.
quest.example: A road tunnel can pass straight through a mountain.

clues: Africa and Antarctica are examples of my category.
I am one of the major divisions of Earth's land.
Many classrooms use a seven-part model, although continent models vary.
quest.example: South America is one of Earth's continents.

clues: I am the planet on which we live.
My surface includes oceans and continents.
I orbit the Sun and have one natural moon.
quest.example: Earth is the planet where we live.

clues: I am the apparent boundary between the visible sky and land or water.
My position depends on the observer and surrounding terrain.
I am an apparent visual boundary, not a flow of water.
quest.example: At sea, the distant water seems to touch the sky.

clues: I am a group or chain of islands.
My members can be volcanic, coral-built, or made by other processes.
I name the collection rather than one long sea inlet.
quest.example: Indonesia is an archipelago of many islands.

clues: I am a ringlike coral reef or coral-island formation surrounding a lagoon.
I commonly develop in tropical seas as volcanic islands subside and reefs grow.
My defining clue is the reef-ring and lagoon arrangement.
quest.example: Some Maldives islands form rings around lagoons.

clues: My regional name is used for a slow-moving or stagnant waterway, often in lowlands.
Louisiana has many named examples.
I can be a channel, creek, or wetland-connected waterway; the name is regional.
quest.example: Slow, winding bayous run through Louisiana.
quest.note: I can be a channel, creek, or wetland-connected waterway; the name is regional.

clues: In a stream network, my word can name a smaller watercourse or fork.
My channel can connect with other channels in a drainage network.
My name overlaps with tributary and stream in some regions.
quest.example: A small branch of a river joins the main flow.
quest.note: My name overlaps with tributary and stream in some regions.

clues: I am waves that become unstable and topple forward.
My crest collapses into foam, often in shallow water near a shore.
I name the breaking waves, not the whole ocean.
quest.example: Breaking waves crash into white foam near beaches.

clues: I am a passage or elongated route through which water flows or vessels travel.
I may be natural or artificially modified.
A canal can be a built kind of me; the terms need not be opposites.
quest.example: Ships follow deep channels through shallow waters.

clues: I am the submerged, relatively shallow margin of a continent.
I extend seaward from the coast toward a steeper continental slope.
I am underwater continental land, not a narrow connection between landmasses.
quest.example: The continental shelf lies under shallow sea near shore.

clues: I am all the land from which runoff drains to a common outlet.
Streams within me join a connected drainage system.
Watershed is often a synonym for me; the two must not be treated as exclusive answers.
quest.example: Rain over a drainage basin flows to one river.
quest.note: Watershed is often a synonym for me; the two must not be treated as exclusive answers.

clues: I am a coastal waterbody where seawater and freshwater mix in many familiar examples.
Rivers deliver freshwater while the sea supplies salt water.
Some estuaries have unusual salinity patterns; my common river-sea setting is the clue here.
quest.example: Chesapeake Bay is an estuary where fresh and salt water mix.

clues: I am a long, narrow inlet occupying a glacier-carved valley.
Steep valley walls commonly rise above my sea water.
My glacial origin distinguishes this example from an ordinary shallow coastal pool.
quest.example: Norway has fjords cut by ancient glaciers.

clues: I am relatively flat land alongside a river that can be covered during floods.
River sediment may build parts of my surface over time.
I am adjoining land, not the flowing channel itself.
quest.example: When a river overtops its banks, water spreads across the low ground beside it.

clues: I am projecting coastal land, often with relatively high or steep sides.
My land juts beyond neighboring shoreline into water.
Cape overlaps with my meaning; these coastal names are not strict opposites.
quest.example: A rocky headland reaches out beyond a coast.
quest.note: Cape overlaps with my meaning; these coastal names are not strict opposites.

clues: I am a narrow entry or arm of water extending into land.
I connect a larger waterbody to a smaller water area or indent the coast.
Bay and cove can overlap with my meaning; shape and local naming matter.
quest.example: A narrow inlet lets sea water reach into land.
quest.note: Bay and cove can overlap with my meaning; shape and local naming matter.

clues: I am relatively shallow water separated from a larger sea by a barrier such as a reef or sandbar.
My barrier may still leave openings through which water moves.
The barrier is the key clue, not simply the fact that I am a coastal pool.
quest.example: A shallow lagoon may sit behind a coral reef.

clues: I am a pronounced bend in a river or stream channel.
Flow can erode my outer bank and deposit sediment on my inner bank.
A series of my curves gives a river a winding path.
quest.example: A river curves through its floodplain in a series of sweeping bends.

clues: I can form when a looping river bend is cut off from its main channel.
My waterbody often has a curved or horseshoe shape.
I preserve part of a former meander rather than marking a river's source.
quest.example: A river cuts across a bend, leaving a curved lake beside its newer, straighter channel.

clues: I am a ridge or accumulation of sand deposited in or across water.
Currents and waves can build me in a river, estuary, or coastal area.
I may be submerged or exposed depending on water level.
quest.example: A sandbar may form near a river mouth.

clues: I am a place where groundwater emerges naturally at the ground surface.
My water may feed a stream or pool.
I describe water reaching the surface, rather than the underground material storing it.
quest.example: Groundwater emerges on a hillside and feeds a small stream.

clues: I am a narrow water passage connecting larger waterbodies.
Land lies on either side of my passage.
Gibraltar is a named example; an isthmus is the land connection instead.
quest.example: The Strait of Gibraltar is narrow water between lands.

clues: I am the periodic rise and fall of water level caused mainly by gravitational interactions with the Moon and Sun.
My timing and size vary by location.
I describe a water-level cycle, not a floating mass of ice.
quest.example: High tide lifts the water higher along a beach.

clues: I commonly mean land whose runoff drains to a shared outlet.
In some regions my word instead names the divide between drainage areas.
Drainage basin is a common synonym for my first meaning; local usage should be explained.
quest.example: Rain in a watershed drains toward the same water system.
quest.note: Drainage basin is a common synonym for my first meaning; local usage should be explained.

clues: I am a low or depressed land area, often surrounded by higher ground.
Some examples collect water; others remain dry.
My bowl-like shape does not by itself mean that all water drains to one river.
quest.example: A low basin can collect rainwater after a storm.

clues: I am a steep bank or broad steep face overlooking lower ground or water.
A river can erode a bank and leave one of me.
Cliff overlaps with my meaning; local naming and shape matter.
quest.example: Some tall bluffs overlook the Mississippi River.
quest.note: Cliff overlaps with my meaning; local naming and shape matter.

clues: I am a deep, steep-sided opening or gap in rock or ground.
A fracture or erosion can help form an example.
Canyon and gorge can overlap with my description; naming is not a strict width test.
quest.example: A deep chasm splits rock with steep sides.
quest.note: Canyon and gorge can overlap with my description; naming is not a strict width test.

clues: I am a volcanic cone built largely from loose erupted fragments.
Cinders and other material pile around a vent.
I am a type of volcano, rather than a desert landform defined by rainfall.
quest.example: A cinder cone volcano is built from small rock pieces.

clues: I am a deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
Flowing water can cut me into rock.
Canyon overlaps with my meaning; the two do not have a universal width boundary.
quest.example: A river may run through a steep rocky gorge.
quest.note: Canyon overlaps with my meaning; the two do not have a universal width boundary.

clues: I am an isolated elevated landform with a relatively flat top and steep sides.
My name comes from a Spanish word for table.
Plateau overlaps in appearance, but my isolated table-like setting is the clue here.
quest.example: A mesa looks like a table standing in a desert.
quest.note: Plateau overlaps in appearance, but my isolated table-like setting is the clue here.

clues: I am an accumulation of debris transported or left by a glacier.
Rock and sediment may pile along the side or end of the ice.
My glacial origin distinguishes me from a dune built chiefly by wind.
quest.example: A ridge of mixed stones and sediment remains along the margin of a retreating glacier.

clues: I am a peat-forming wetland typically fed mostly by precipitation.
Sphagnum moss commonly grows in my wet, often acidic conditions.
Peat is partly decayed plant material that builds up in me.
quest.example: A bog can feel spongy because of wet moss.

clues: I am a temperate grassland type associated especially with North America.
Grasses dominate and trees are generally sparse away from wetter locations.
I describe a grassland ecosystem, not just any small grassy field.
quest.example: Tall grasses wave across the North American prairie.

clues: I am a cold biome with a short growing season and little or no tall-tree cover.
Low shrubs, grasses, mosses, and lichens can grow in me.
Arctic and alpine examples exist; permafrost is common in Arctic examples but not universal.
quest.example: Arctic tundra has few trees and short summers.
quest.note: Arctic and alpine examples exist; permafrost is common in Arctic examples but not universal.

clues: I am land where water at or near the surface strongly shapes soil and life.
Marshes, swamps, and bogs are examples of my broad category.
My plants and soils are adapted to saturated conditions.
quest.example: Waterlogged ground supports plants adapted to saturated soil.

clues: I am an embankment that runs along a riverbank rather than blocking the channel across its flow.
I usually run alongside the water rather than blocking its channel.
Some examples form naturally as a river deposits sediment on its banks.
quest.example: A levee beside a river helps block floodwater.

clues: I am a gated water chamber used to raise or lower boats.
Water fills or drains from my chamber to match the next level.
I let boats pass between different water levels on a canal or river.
quest.example: Canal locks raise and lower boats using gates.

clues: My water is stored for a planned use such as supply, irrigation, or power.
A dam can create one kind of me, but storage sites take other forms too.
I am the stored-water body or storage place, not the barrier holding it.
quest.example: Lake Mead is a reservoir that stores water.

clues: I am a built waterside structure used for loading, unloading, or mooring vessels.
I often run along a bank or shoreline, though port terminology varies.
Pier overlaps with my meaning; neither word guarantees a single construction shape.
quest.example: Ships load and unload cargo at a wharf.
quest.note: Pier overlaps with my meaning; neither word guarantees a single construction shape.

clues: I describe vertical height relative to a reference surface.
An aircraft's height above mean sea level is one use of my word.
Elevation overlaps with my meaning, so this is not a strict land-versus-air rule.
quest.example: A plane might fly at an altitude of 10,000 feet.
quest.note: Elevation overlaps with my meaning, so this is not a strict land-versus-air rule.

clues: I am a map symbol that displays directions.
North, south, east, and west may be arranged around my center.
I help a reader orient a map; I do not measure distance.
quest.example: A compass rose on a park map helps a walker identify north, south, east and west.

clues: On a map, I connect points at equal elevation.
Several of me can show a hill's shape.
Closely spaced examples usually indicate a steeper slope than widely spaced ones.
quest.example: A contour labeled 100 meters joins map positions at that elevation.

clues: I am a set of values used to locate a position.
A latitude-longitude pair is one example of me.
Different coordinate systems use different axes and units.
quest.example: A map location can be specified with a latitude such as 20°N and a longitude such as 10°E.

clues: I describe a location's height relative to a vertical reference such as sea level.
A contour label can give my value for ground on a map.
Altitude overlaps with my meaning; context helps explain the intended usage.
quest.example: Denver is about 5,280 feet above sea level.
quest.note: Altitude overlaps with my meaning; context helps explain the intended usage.

clues: An imaginary line circles Earth halfway between its geographic poles.
Its latitude is zero degrees.
It divides the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
quest.example: On a classroom globe, zero degrees latitude circles the middle between the poles.

clues: My word means half of a sphere.
Earth can be divided into northern and southern examples.
An eastern or western half of Earth is another way to describe me.
quest.example: The equator divides a globe into northern and southern halves.

clues: I measure angular distance north or south of the equator.
My value runs from zero to ninety degrees north or south.
On a globe, parallels mark positions with the same value of me.
quest.example: A point at 20°N is north of the equator; a point at 20°S is south of it.

clues: I measure angular position east or west of a prime meridian.
Lines representing equal values of me run between Earth's poles.
Latitude uses north-south distance from the equator; I use east-west position.
quest.example: Two locations at 10°E lie on the same meridian, even if one is farther north.

clues: I explain what a map's symbols and colors mean.
I might tell you that a blue line means a river.
Map legend is another name for me.
quest.example: A map key might explain that a dotted line marks a walking path and a blue patch marks water.

clues: I relate a distance on a map to a distance in the real world.
I may appear as a ratio, a written statement, or a marked bar.
If one centimeter stands for one kilometer, that relationship is an example of me.
quest.example: If a map uses 1 centimeter for 1 kilometer, a 3-centimeter route represents 3 kilometers.

clues: I am the northern end of Earth's rotation axis at the surface.
My latitude is ninety degrees north.
The geographic point named here is different from the moving magnetic north pole.
quest.example: The northern end of Earth’s rotation axis meets the surface at the North Pole.

clues: I am the southern end of Earth's rotation axis at the surface.
My latitude is ninety degrees south.
My geographic point lies on Antarctica, rather than in the Arctic Ocean.
quest.example: The southern end of Earth’s rotation axis meets the surface at the South Pole.

clues: I portray the shape and elevation of land on a map.
Contour lines are a familiar tool I use to show relief.
I can help a walker locate ridges, valleys, and steep slopes.
quest.example: A walker uses contour patterns on a topographic map to spot a steep hillside.

clues: I am underground rock or sediment that can store and transmit usable groundwater.
Water occupies connected pores or fractures in me.
A well can draw groundwater from me; I am not necessarily an underground lake.
quest.example: A well draws groundwater from water-filled pores in sand or cracks in rock.

clues: I occur when transported sediment is laid down.
A river may leave sand behind when its flow slows.
I build sediment deposits rather than carrying them away.
quest.example: A river slows and leaves a sandbar beside its channel.

clues: I involve moving soil, sediment, or rock material from one place to another.
Water, wind, ice, and gravity can transport the material.
Weathering breaks material down; I carry it away.
quest.example: After rain, a stream carries loosened sand downstream.

clues: I am a hot spring that intermittently ejects water and steam.
Underground heating and a constricted plumbing system help cause my eruptions.
Old Faithful is a named example.
quest.example: Hot water erupts periodically from a vent at the ground’s surface.
quest.note: A geyser is a kind of hot spring; it is distinguished by its erupting water and steam.

clues: I am a natural spring whose water is heated underground.
Geothermal heat warms the groundwater that reaches my surface.
Unlike a geyser, I need not erupt periodically.
quest.example: Groundwater heated below the surface emerges in a warm pool.
quest.note: A geyser is a kind of hot spring. A hot spring does not have to erupt periodically.

clues: I break down or alter rock where it is.
Freezing water, chemicals, and living things can help cause me.
Erosion involves transport; I do not require the broken material to move away.
quest.example: Water freezes inside a rock crack and helps widen it without transporting the rock away.

compare.explanation: Both are inland waterbodies. Pond often suggests smaller or shallower water, but there is no universal lake-versus-pond size boundary; local names can overlap.
compare.example: Lake Michigan is a very large lake. A duck pond in a neighborhood park.

compare.explanation: Water is all around an island. A peninsula stays connected to land.
compare.example: Hawaii has many islands surrounded by ocean. Florida sticks out into the Atlantic and Gulf waters.

compare.explanation: Stream is a broad term for channelized flowing water. Rivers, creeks, and brooks can all be streams; their names do not follow a universal size boundary.
compare.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States. A small stream runs through a wooded park.

compare.explanation: Both rise above surrounding land. Mountain often suggests greater relief, but there is no universal height separating a mountain from a hill.
compare.example: Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas. A rounded grassy hill in a park.

compare.explanation: Valley is the broader low-land corridor. Canyons are steep-sided valleys; a feature may correctly be called both. Gorge overlaps with canyon.
compare.example: Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls. The Grand Canyon has deep sides carved by a river.

compare.explanation: A forest has many trees. A meadow is open and grassy.
compare.example: The Amazon Rainforest has millions of trees. A meadow covered in grass and wildflowers.

compare.explanation: Oceans are vast connected salt-water bodies. Lakes are inland waterbodies enclosed by land apart from inlets and outlets. Some lakes are salty, so fresh versus salty is not a universal test.
compare.example: The Pacific Ocean covers a huge part of Earth. Lake Michigan is a very large lake.

compare.explanation: Beach describes a shore deposit of loose sand, gravel, or pebbles. Cliff describes a steep face. A beach can lie at the base of a cliff.
compare.example: A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida. The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.

compare.explanation: A waterfall has a distinct abrupt drop or series of drops. Rapids describe a fast turbulent reach of flowing water. Both can occur along the same river.
compare.example: Niagara Falls pours over a steep drop. Whitewater rapids tumble over rocks in rivers.

compare.explanation: Both are wetlands. A typical swamp has prominent woody vegetation, while a typical marsh is dominated by nonwoody plants. Vegetation, rather than wetness alone, is the useful distinction.
compare.example: Cypress trees can grow in a flooded swamp. Grassy marshes grow in the Florida Everglades.

compare.explanation: A desert gets little rain. An oasis is a watered spot in a dry area.
compare.example: The Sahara Desert receives very little rainfall. An oasis may have palms and a pool in a desert.

compare.explanation: A source is where a river starts. Its mouth is where it ends in another water body.
compare.example: A mountain spring may be a river's source. The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

compare.explanation: Upstream points toward a river's start. Downstream follows the water's flow.
compare.example: A canoe going upstream travels toward a river's start. A floating leaf goes downstream with the current.

compare.explanation: Shore is adjoining land; shoreline is the boundary where water and land meet. Their exact extent changes with water level and usage.
compare.example: The shore of a lake is where its water meets land. A lake's shoreline curves around its edges.

compare.explanation: A summit is a mountain's highest point. A valley is low land between hills or mountains.
compare.example: A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit. Yosemite Valley sits between high rocky walls.

compare.explanation: Cave describes a natural cavity in rock. Tunnel describes a passage through an obstruction; many tunnels are built, but natural tunnels also exist.
compare.example: Mammoth Cave has underground passages. A road tunnel can pass straight through a mountain.

compare.explanation: A hill can be made of different earth or rock. A dune is a hill of sand.
compare.example: A rounded grassy hill in a park. Sand dunes rise in Colorado's Great Sand Dunes.

compare.explanation: A glacier moves slowly on land. An iceberg floats in water.
compare.example: A glacier slowly moves down an Alaskan valley. Icebergs float in the cold North Atlantic Ocean.

compare.explanation: Bay and gulf are overlapping conventional names for coastal water partly enclosed by land. Gulf often suggests a large indentation, but there is no universal size distinction.
compare.example: San Francisco Bay curves into the land. The Gulf of Mexico is partly surrounded by land.

compare.explanation: A pier is a built platform reaching into water. A harbor is sheltered water for boats.
compare.example: A fishing pier reaches out over the ocean. New York Harbor provides sheltered water for ships.

compare.explanation: Woods have many trees. A field is open land.
compare.example: A small patch of woods behind a house. A grassy field where children play soccer.

compare.explanation: Both can be flat. A plateau stands high above surrounding land.
compare.example: The Great Plains spread across central North America. The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.

compare.explanation: Summit names the highest point of a feature. Peak often suggests a pointed high point; a feature can be both a peak and a summit, and usage varies.
compare.example: A pointed mountain peak sticks up into the clouds. A climber might stand on Mount Everest's summit.

compare.explanation: Coast usually refers to the land-ocean zone. Shore also applies beside lakes and rivers. The terms overlap on an ocean coastline.
compare.example: Florida's Atlantic coast is next to the ocean. The shore of a lake is where its water meets land.

compare.explanation: A current is directed water flow. A wave carries a disturbance through water; water particles also move, so waves do not mean motionless water.
compare.example: An ocean current carries water along the coast. Ocean waves roll toward a beach and rise and fall.

compare.explanation: A volcano has an opening where melted rock may come out. Not every mountain is a volcano.
compare.example: Mount St. Helens in Washington is a volcano. Mount Everest rises high in the Himalayas.

compare.explanation: River describes a kind of flowing watercourse. Tributary describes its relationship to a receiving watercourse. A river can also be a tributary.
compare.example: The Mississippi River winds across the United States. The Missouri River joins the Mississippi River.

compare.explanation: A beach is loose shore sediment. A sandbar is an accumulation in or across water; changing water levels can expose it and connect it to a beach.
compare.example: A sandbar may form near a river mouth. A sandy Atlantic Ocean beach in Florida.

compare.explanation: A dam is a barrier controlling water. A reservoir is a place or body in which water is stored. Many reservoirs are behind dams, but the terms name different things.
compare.example: Hoover Dam holds back water in a river. Lake Mead is a reservoir that stores water.

compare.explanation: The mouth is where a river empties. A delta is land made from sediment near some river mouths.
compare.example: The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf. The Mississippi River empties into the Gulf of Mexico.

compare.explanation: An estuary is a coastal waterbody with river-sea interaction in familiar examples. A delta is a sediment deposit near a river mouth. An estuary and delta can occur together.
compare.example: Chesapeake Bay is an estuary where fresh and salt water mix. The Mississippi River makes a delta near the Gulf.

compare.explanation: Archipelago describes a group of islands. Atoll describes a ringlike coral-reef or coral-island arrangement around a lagoon. Some atolls contain multiple islands and can also be archipelagos.
compare.example: Some Maldives islands form rings around lagoons. Indonesia is an archipelago of many islands.

compare.explanation: A strait is skinny water between lands. An isthmus is skinny land between waters.
compare.example: The Strait of Gibraltar is narrow water between lands. The Isthmus of Panama links two larger land areas.

compare.explanation: Bluff often names a steep bank overlooking lower land or water. Cliff is a broader steep-face term. The names overlap and local usage matters.
compare.example: Some tall bluffs overlook the Mississippi River. The Cliffs of Moher rise above the ocean in Ireland.

compare.explanation: A fjord is long, narrow, and carved by ice. A cove is a small sheltered bay.
compare.example: Norway has fjords cut by ancient glaciers. A small sheltered cove might hold tiny boats.

compare.explanation: A levee runs beside water to stop flooding. A dam crosses a waterway to hold water back.
compare.example: A levee beside a river helps block floodwater. Hoover Dam holds back water in a river.

compare.explanation: A watershed is land draining into a water system. A river is flowing water in that system.
compare.example: Rain in a watershed drains toward the same water system. The Mississippi River winds across the United States.

compare.explanation: Both refer to height relative to a reference. Elevation is commonly used for ground locations and altitude for aircraft, but that convention is not an exclusive scientific rule.
compare.example: Denver is about 5,280 feet above sea level. A plane might fly at an altitude of 10,000 feet.

compare.explanation: Both can be elevated and flat-topped. Mesa often suggests an isolated table-like feature with steep sides. Plateau commonly describes a broader elevated region, without a universal size cutoff.
compare.example: A mesa looks like a table standing in a desert. The Colorado Plateau is a broad high land area.

compare.explanation: Channel is a broad passage or watercourse term. A canal is a built or substantially modified waterway, so it can also be a channel.
compare.example: Ships travel through the Panama Canal. Ships follow deep channels through shallow waters.

compare.explanation: Latitude measures angular position north or south of the equator; longitude measures angular position east or west of a prime meridian. Together they can locate a point.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Weathering breaks down or alters rock in place. Erosion transports material. Weathered material can later be eroded.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Erosion transports material away; deposition lays transported material down. A river can erode one bank and deposit sediment elsewhere.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: An aquifer is permeable rock or sediment storing and transmitting groundwater. A spring is a place where groundwater emerges at the surface.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Both involve geothermally heated groundwater. A geyser intermittently ejects water and steam; a hot spring need not erupt. A geyser is a special kind of hot spring.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: The river is flowing water in its channel. A floodplain is adjoining land that can be inundated during floods.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A meander is a bend in a flowing channel. An oxbow lake can occupy a former bend after it is cut off.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Scale relates map distance to real distance. A key explains symbols and colors.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A contour connects equal elevations on a map. A meridian represents equal longitude on Earth.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: These are opposite surface ends of Earth’s rotation axis. Geographic poles differ from magnetic poles.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A glacier is moving land ice. A moraine is debris transported or deposited by glacier ice.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: Wetland is the broad saturated-land category. Marsh is one wetland type, typically dominated by nonwoody plants.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: The equator is a zero-latitude reference line. A hemisphere is half of a sphere; the equator separates Earth’s northern and southern halves.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A source is a river’s beginning. A spring is groundwater emerging naturally; it may supply a river’s source, but not every source is a spring.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.

compare.explanation: A dune is shaped chiefly by wind-deposited sand. A moraine consists of debris associated with a glacier.
compare.example: Try explaining the relationship in your own words, then name an example.
